claims.text: Refining CoCrFeMnNi from a coarse-grained to a nanocrystalline state increases grain-boundary density.
Higher grain-boundary density accelerates formation of a protective passive oxide layer.
Higher grain-boundary density accelerates repair of a mechanically damaged passive oxide layer.
Passive-film self-healing governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion.
The passive-film mechanism provides tribocorrosion resistance when repassivation is faster than mechanical oxide removal.
Severe plastic deformation can transform coarse-grained equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi into a nanocrystalline state.
Grain boundaries act as nucleation sites for oxide formation in nanocrystalline CoCrFeMnNi.
The increased grain-boundary density produces a rapidly regenerating, stable passive tribolayer.
Accelerated repassivation produces a continuous protective oxide film that repairs wear-induced damage.
Nanocrystalline CoCrFeMnNi will have lower friction than coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi under matched tribocorrosion conditions.
Nanocrystalline CoCrFeMnNi will have lower wear depth than coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi under matched tribocorrosion conditions.
Nanocrystalline CoCrFeMnNi will have lower corrosion current than coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi under matched tribocorrosion conditions.
The predicted benefits diminish when mechanical oxide removal exceeds repassivation.
The predicted nanocrystalline benefit should hold under moderate loads for which repassivation can counteract wear.
The nanocrystalline benefit may vanish under loads that damage the oxide faster than it reforms.
Failure of the nanocrystalline sample to show faster repassivation or lower wear and corrosion metrics than the matched coarse-grained control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
